records.issue_text: [BUG] The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` before identity resolution, while the permission cache key path resolves the user via `s.GetUserIdentifiers` and keys on `userIdentifiers.UID`, so the two caches use different subjects whenever the request's UserUID is not already the canonical UID. When a Check arrives with a UserUID that resolves (via idCache/store lookup) to a different canonical UID, the denial entry is written under the raw request UID while the permission cache lives under the resolved UID; the denial is then never covered by any subject-keyed invalidation and can deny a user whose permissions were just changed, and conversely misses dedup opportunities.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The new negative (denial) result cache has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff, so a grant of permission after a denial keeps the user locked out for the full shortCacheTTL window. An admin grants a user access (or a permission is edited) after the user was denied once for (namespace, user, action, name, folder); every subsequent Check for that resource keeps returning {Allowed: false} from permDenialCache until the TTL expires, because no permission-change/invalidation hook in this diff deletes userPermDenialCacheKey entries — the existing invalidation paths only know about userPermCacheKey. This is under-scoping of the stated caching intent: caching was added without the invalidation requirement that already applies to the positive-permission cache.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The denial cache is consulted before the subject is resolved/validated, so it returns a deny for key components taken directly from the request (Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.ParentFolder) without the UID resolution the positive path performs via GetUserIdentifiers. Two Check requests that resolve to different actual users but carry colliding raw UserUID/folder strings in the same namespace would share a denial entry; more practically, the deny path never verifies the identity mapping, so the code path enforces a weaker invariant than the allow path it sits beside. Operators debugging 'user denied despite correct role' are bitten when the pre-identity denial short-circuits.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The cached-denial short-circuit and the cached-permission allow path both return before consulting s.identityStore-based freshness or running the singleflight/DB path, but the denial Set at lines 153-155 fires even when the deny came from a stale/outdated permCache fallback that already hit the DB — meaning a deny is cached under a key that mixes namespace+user+action+name+parent while the DB result it was derived from was authoritative, yet the earlier cache-miss path in the same request may have returned an allow from stale cache in a prior request, producing inconsistent cached allow/deny states for the same resource within the TTL window. Within shortCacheTTL, two identical Check requests for the same resource can return contradictory results (allowed from stale permCache vs denied from denial cache populated by a later DB check), and callers cannot tell which is authoritative; anyone relying on monotonic permission changes within the TTL window gets flapping authorization decisions.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates unbounded user-supplied components (name, parent from the CheckRequest) into a cache key with a fixed '.'/'_' separator scheme that can collide with userPermCacheKey's format when fields contain underscores. Two distinct (name, parent) pairs such as ('a_b','c') and ('a','b_c') map to the same key, so a denial recorded for one resource denies a different resource for the same user until TTL expiry — a correctness/security drift an attacker controlling dashboard or folder names can trigger to deny access to other resources in their org.
